questions.question: How many paths of travel does each traffic lane provide for a motorcyclist?
questions.explanation: Each traffic lane has three paths for motorcyclists: left, center, and right.

questions.question: What is the proper footwear for riding a motorcycle?
questions.explanation: Wear sturdy shoes with short heels that cover your ankles. Tall heels can catch on things. Tuck in any loose laces so they don't get caught.

questions.question: What does this hand signal mean?
questions.explanation: When the left arm is bent at the elbow and points downward, it means the rider is slowing down or stopping.

questions.question: When crossing angled railroad tracks, what is the safest approach?
questions.explanation: Go straight in your lane when crossing angled railroad tracks. Turning to reach a right angle can push you into another lane.

questions.question: How should you park a motorcycle next to a curb?

options.text: At a 90-degree angle with the rear wheel touching the curb
At a 45-degree angle with the front tire touching the curb
Like a car, with both wheels the same distance from the curb
At the left edge of the space so drivers can see it better

questions.correctAnswerText: At a 90-degree angle with the rear wheel touching the curb
questions.explanation: Park at a 90-degree angle to the curb with your rear wheel touching it.

questions.question: How do you do maximum straight-line braking?

options.text: Use the front brake first, then the rear brake
Use the rear brake first, then the front brake
Use both brakes at the same time without locking either wheel
Use both brakes at the same time while locking the rear wheel

questions.correctAnswerText: Use both brakes at the same time without locking either wheel
questions.explanation: Use the front and rear brakes together at the same time without locking either wheel.

questions.question: If road conditions require longer stopping distance, what should you do?
questions.explanation: Increase your following distance if your motorcycle needs more distance to stop. Keep at least a three-second distance on slippery roads or in heavy traffic.

questions.question: What should you do to be more visible at an intersection?

options.text: Make eye contact with other drivers

questions.explanation: Keep your headlight on and ride in a lane position that makes you easy to see. Never assume another driver sees you, even if you make eye contact.

questions.question: What should a passenger do when getting on a motorcycle?

options.text: Sit as far back as possible

questions.explanation: Mount after the engine starts and the transmission is in neutral. Sit as far forward as you can without blocking the rider, and hold onto the rider's waist, hips, or belt.

questions.question: When passing another vehicle on the left, which part of the lane should you ride in?
questions.explanation: Ride in the left portion of the lane when passing on the left. This helps you see ahead and makes you more visible to oncoming traffic.

questions.question: When the motorcycle's weight moves forward while braking, what can you do?

options.text: Use less pressure on the front brake.

questions.explanation: When your weight shifts forward during braking, the front wheel gets more traction. This means you can press the front brake harder.

questions.question: What should you do to reduce your reaction time?

options.text: Keep your hand near the clutch and brakes.
Shift into neutral when slowing down.

questions.correctAnswerText: Keep your hand near the clutch and brakes.
questions.explanation: When approaching a risky area like an intersection, position your hand near the clutch and brakes. This helps you react faster if danger appears.

questions.question: When looking through a turn, what should you do?
questions.explanation: Look through the turn toward where you want to go. Turn only your head, not your shoulders. Keep your eyes level with the horizon.

questions.question: Where should inexperienced riders position themselves in a group?

options.text: At the back of the group.

questions.explanation: Less experienced riders should position themselves just behind the leader. This allows more experienced riders behind them to watch over them.

questions.question: Which of these should you NOT do to prevent fatigue on a long ride?

options.text: Limit how far you ride each day.

questions.explanation: Dress to protect yourself from tiring weather like wind and rain. Ride no more than six hours per day and take a break at least every two hours. Do not use artificial stimulants because extreme fatigue can hit when they wear off.

questions.question: What is the best group formation for curves, turns, or entering a highway?
questions.explanation: While staggered formation works for normal riding, switch to single-file when going through curves, turns, or entering or leaving a highway.

questions.question: When is it most important to flash your brake light?

options.text: When you are about to slow down suddenly.
When there is a stop sign ahead.
When your turn signals are not working.

questions.correctAnswerText: When you are about to slow down suddenly.
questions.explanation: Flash your brake light before slowing suddenly, especially if a vehicle is following you too closely. The driver may not notice hazards ahead that you are slowing down to avoid.

questions.question: What should you do when braking on a slippery surface?

options.text: Do not brake. Just downshift instead.

questions.explanation: On slippery surfaces, slow down and avoid sudden moves. Use both brakes when you need to slow down or stop.

questions.question: Which is NOT a benefit of riding in a close group?

options.text: The group takes up less space on the highway.
The group is easier to see.
The group is less likely to get split up.
A close group will reach the destination faster than a spread-out group.

questions.correctAnswerText: A close group will reach the destination faster than a spread-out group.
questions.explanation: Riding in a close group takes up less space, is easier to see, and is less likely to get separated at traffic lights. However, being close does not make you reach your destination any faster.

questions.question: What will help you ride safely on slippery surfaces?

options.text: Using the center of the lane.

questions.explanation: Slow down and use both brakes on slippery surfaces. Avoid sudden moves. Stay away from the center of the lane and follow tire tracks left by cars. Watch for things that make roads slippery, like oil and loose gravel.

questions.question: Most motorcycle crashes happen:

options.text: After riding for a long time.

questions.explanation: Most motorcycle crashes happen on short trips under five miles long, traveling at speeds under 30 miles per hour.

questions.question: When riding in a group, where should inexperienced riders be placed?

options.text: In the front of the group.
At the back of the group.

questions.explanation: Inexperienced riders should ride just behind the lead rider. This way, experienced riders can watch them and help keep them safe.

questions.question: Which is a poor reason to sound your horn?

options.text: A driver in the next lane is too close to the vehicle ahead of them.
A person is sitting in a parked car.
You want people to look at your motorcycle.
You are passing a pedestrian in the street.

questions.correctAnswerText: You want people to look at your motorcycle.
questions.explanation: Use your horn to warn other drivers and pedestrians who might move into your path. Sound it when passing vehicles, people in parked cars, or pedestrians in the street. Do not use it just to get attention.

questions.question: To swerve, you should:

options.text: Press the handgrip in the direction of the turn.
Press the handgrip in the opposite direction of the turn.

questions.correctAnswerText: Press the handgrip in the direction of the turn.
questions.explanation: To swerve, press on the handgrip on the side where you want to go. To turn left, press the left handgrip, then the right to straighten out. To turn right, press the right handgrip, then the left.

questions.question: When looking through a turn, you should:

options.text: Turn both your head and your shoulders to get a better look.
Turn just your head, not your shoulders.
Only move your eyes, not your head.

questions.correctAnswerText: Turn just your head, not your shoulders.
questions.explanation: When turning, look ahead to where you want to go. Turn only your head, keep your shoulders still, and keep your eyes level with the horizon.
